sections.history: Tirunaraiyur lies in the Kattumannarkoil country of Cuddalore district, in the Chola heartland north of the Kaveri. The Tevaram hymns of the saints Sambandar and Appar praise the Lord of this town, which makes it a Paadal Petra Sthalam. Its second claim to fame is a person: Nambiyandar Nambi, the temple priest's son who, in the age of the Chola emperor Rajaraja I, is remembered as the one who gathered the scattered Tamil Shaiva hymns into the Tirumurai. The town's name is traditionally read as the place of the crane, from a curse told in its legends. The temple has been enlarged by Chola-era and later patrons, and the exact stages of its building are not firmly recorded.
sections.architecture: A three-tiered rajagopuram faces east. Entering, the visitor meets first the shrine of Polla Pillaiyar, the Ganesha of the temple, and then a mandapam holding the Nandi before the sanctum of Soundareswarar, where the Shiva linga is also known as Siddhanathar. The goddess Thiripurasundari has her own shrine. Around the courtyard are shrines to Murugan, to Gajalakshmi, to the Navagrahas, to Sani, to Bhairava and to Surya. In the main prakara, paintings tell the life of Nambiyandar Nambi, and in the Pillaiyar's sanctum stand images of the saint-scholar and of the king who sought him out.
sections.legends: Two stories mark Tirunaraiyur. The first is the self-manifested Pillaiyar, whose name, understood as Pollappillaiyar, means the Ganesha who was never chiselled. The young Nambi, serving in the temple, offered food to the image each day, but it stayed silent until his devotion moved it to accept. When Rajaraja Chola heard of it he asked to see the miracle, and Nambi sang the Irattai Mani Malai before the Lord took the offering. Tradition adds that the Pillaiyar then guided the king to the hymns hidden in a chamber of the Chidambaram temple, and is honoured as the Thirumurai Kanda Vinayakar. The second story tells of a Gandharva cursed by the sage Durvasa to live as a crane, and gives the town its name.
sections.festivals: The festival most dear to the town is the Vaikasi celebration of Nambiyandar Nambi in May or June, when the hymns of the Tirumurai are chanted in the temple he is remembered for. Vinayaka Chaturthi in August or September draws devotees to the Pillaiyar, and Navaratri and Skanda Sashti are kept with devotion. Maha Shivaratri and the monthly Pradosham are observed as at every Shiva temple. Confirm dates locally, as they follow the Tamil calendar.
sections.experience: Tirunaraiyur rewards a patient, unhurried visit. Enter beneath the east gopuram and greet the self-manifested Polla Pillaiyar first, as devotees have done for centuries, then proceed past Nandi to the sanctum of Soundareswarar and to the shrine of Thiripurasundari. Look at the paintings in the prakara telling the life of Nambi, and pause at the images of Nambi and Rajaraja in the Pillaiyar's sanctum. Students and singers of the Tamil hymns come here to remember the man who gathered them. The temple sits in quiet farming country, and a short walk from the road brings you into its stillness.

visit.timings: Typically open from early morning to around midday and again from the late afternoon into the evening; confirm timings locally, especially on festival days.
visit.dressCode: Modest traditional attire is expected: dhotis or trousers for men, sarees, salwar kameez, or long skirts for women, with shoulders and knees covered. Footwear is left outside the temple.
visit.photography: Photography is generally permitted in the outer corridors and courtyards but prohibited inside the inner sanctum, in keeping with Tamil Nadu temple rules. Ask temple staff before photographing rituals or priests.
visit.gettingThere: Tirunaraiyur lies on the Chidambaram–Kattumannarkoil road via Kumaratchi, about 17 to 19 km from Chidambaram. Alight at the Tirunaraiyur bus stop; a branch road of roughly half a kilometre leads to the temple. Chidambaram is the nearest major railhead, and the airports at Puducherry, Tiruchirappalli and Chennai are some hours away by road. Take care not to confuse this town with the Tirunaraiyur near Kumbakonam.
